title: Jeremiah 47:1–7
context: Jeremiah reports the LORD's word about the Philistines, dated "before Pharaoh struck Gaza"; the text does not say which Pharaoh or when. The LORD pictures an invading force as floodwaters rising out of the north, overwhelming the land. Fathers flee without turning back for their children, and Gaza and Ashkelon are devastated. The oracle closes with a cry to the sword of the LORD to rest, answered by the reply that it cannot rest while the LORD has given it a command. Other prophets also announce judgment on the Philistines, including Zephaniah 2:4–7.

verses.text: The LORD’s word that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck Gaza.
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD’s word that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines." Arminian readers note the time marker, "before Pharaoh struck Gaza," which the text does not explain further.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Philistines had long been Israel's neighbors and enemies. The LORD's word now reaches them as well. The exact historical setting is uncertain, and it is not supplied here.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Behold, waters rise up out of the north, and will become an overflowing stream, and will overflow the land and all that is therein, the city and those who dwell therein. The men will cry, and all the inhabitants of the land will wail.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says: "Behold, waters rise up out of the north." Arminian readers see the invader pictured as an overflowing stream, sweeping over "the city and those who dwell therein."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image reverses Egypt's boast in 46:8 of rising like the Nile. Now the flood comes from the north. The LORD directs the waters of judgment.

verses.text: At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his strong ones, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of his wheels, the fathers don’t look back for their children because their hands are so feeble,
verses.arminianNotes: "At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his strong ones." Arminian readers see terror so great that "the fathers don’t look back for their children because their hands are so feeble."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the scene shows how judgment breaks even the strongest natural bonds. The LORD's warnings are severe because the reality of war is terrible.

verses.text: because of the day that comes to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper who remains; for the LORD will destroy the Philistines, the remnant of the isle of Caphtor.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks "because of the day that comes to destroy all the Philistines." Arminian readers see the LORD's judgment reaching the Philistines and cutting off "every helper" from Tyre and Sidon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase "the remnant of the isle of Caphtor." Amos 9:7 and Deuteronomy 2:23 also connect the Philistines with Caphtor. These notes name the link without speculating on its location.

verses.text: Baldness has come on Gaza; Ashkelon is brought to nothing. You remnant of their valley, how long will you cut yourself?
verses.arminianNotes: "Baldness has come on Gaza." Arminian readers see signs of mourning in Gaza and Ashkelon, whose people shave their heads and cut themselves in grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the question, "how long will you cut yourself?" The mourning customs show the depth of the disaster. Zephaniah 2:4 also announces that "Gaza will be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation."

verses.text: “ ‘You sword of the LORD, how long will it be before you are quiet? Put yourself back into your scabbard; rest, and be still.’
verses.arminianNotes: "You sword of the LORD, how long will it be before you are quiet?" Arminian readers hear a cry for the sword of judgment to return to its scabbard and rest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the speaker of this cry is not named. It may express the grief of the victims or of the prophet. Either way, it longs for an end to the slaughter.

verses.text: “How can you be quiet, since the LORD has given you a command? Against Ashkelon, and against the seashore, there he has appointed it.”
verses.arminianNotes: "How can you be quiet, since the LORD has given you a command?" Arminian readers see the answer: the sword cannot rest because the LORD has appointed it against Ashkelon and the seashore.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Jeremiah 12:12, where "the sword of the LORD devours." The sword acts only under the LORD's command. Both traditions treat God's rule over judgment as shared ground.
